subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
passage: I am Shalini and I sit next to Arohi in art class. Last Monday she told me she was starting to draw for real. I expected a huge plan, but she said, "Ten minutes a day, that is all. My cousin planned two hours daily and stopped by Thursday. A tiny habit that carries on beats a big one that dies." Every afternoon after that I saw her at the window seat with her sketchbook and a timer on the sill, drawing pots and shoes until it beeped. She stopped even when she was halfway through a leaf. By the third week her sketchbook was fat. I cannot tell if she ever wanted to do more; she just kept going.

qa.q: How many minutes a day did Arohi decide to draw?
qa.a: Arohi decided to draw for ten minutes a day.

qa.q: What was Arohi worried about when she chose such a small amount?
qa.a: That a big plan would fail after a few days, as her cousin's did, so she wanted a habit that would carry on.

qa.q: What could Arohi do when ten minutes starts to feel easy?
qa.a: Add a few minutes slowly or set a small goal, such as one finished drawing a week, because growth stays steady that way.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Arohi stopping halfway through a leaf?
qa.a: With some puzzlement and admiration for the discipline, though Shalini admits she cannot tell whether Arohi wanted to do more.

grounding: A girl beginning drawing chooses ten minutes a day, judging a small habit that continues better than a big plan that stops.

passage: My name is Amandeep, and this is about the week I did not paint. On Monday I decided to become a painter, so I drew a timetable with six colours of pen. On Tuesday I bought brushes and a tube of every colour with my pocket money. On Wednesday I covered the timetable in stickers. By Saturday I had a beautiful chart and a box of new paints, and my friend Thomas asked, "Can I see your first painting?" I opened the sketchbook and looked at the clean white pages. There was nothing on them. I had spent a whole week getting ready to start, and I had mistaken that for starting.

qa.q: How many colours of pen did Amandeep use for the timetable?
qa.a: Amandeep used six colours of pen.

qa.q: What did Amandeep feel when Thomas asked to see a painting?
qa.a: Caught out and a little embarrassed, since there was nothing on the pages after a week of preparing. 😅

qa.q: What could Amandeep do first to actually start?
qa.a: Paint something small for ten minutes today, even if it is messy, because doing it beats more planning.

qa.q: How might Thomas see that week?
qa.a: As all preparation and no painting, though Thomas asked kindly and simply wanted to see a first attempt.

grounding: Amandeep spends a week on a colourful timetable and new supplies but never paints, mistaking planning for progress.

subtype: Approach: tracking progress with a chart [Action]
passage: My name is Alka, and learning to skate felt slower than a snail. Some weeks I fell more than I glided. Coach Kamal said, "Mark a star on your calendar each day you practise." So I stuck one on my wall, and after every session, helmet and pads on, I drew a gold star. On bad days I still drew the star, even if I had only rolled to the gate and back. By the third week there was a row of stars like a fence. When I felt like quitting I looked at the row and thought, that is a lot of showing up. Last Sunday I did a full turn without putting a hand down.

qa.q: Who suggested putting a star on the calendar?
qa.a: Coach Kamal suggested it.

qa.q: How did the row of stars make Alka feel when feeling like quitting?
qa.a: Alka felt encouraged, because the row was proof of a lot of showing up even when progress felt slow.

qa.q: What could Alka add to the chart to see skill as well as effort?
qa.a: Write one thing learned beside each star, because it shows improvement and not just the number of days.

qa.q: How might Coach Kamal see the calendar?
qa.a: As a helpful sign of regular practice, since the coach can see the effort at a glance.

grounding: A learner marks a star for each practice day, and the growing row keeps Alka going through slow weeks.

subtype: Approach: dropping the routine when exams come [Revision]
passage: Note, Friday, from Vikas, art teacher. Chitra came after class to say her exams start in three weeks and she wants to cut painting to Sundays only. I expected to hear she was quitting. Her voice was steady, but her hands were tight around her sketchbook. "Only until the exams finish," she said. "Then I will be back at full pace." Her friend Chetan, waiting at the door, asked if she would still join the December show. She said yes. I told Chitra this is a sensible change and not a giving up, and I reserved her wall space and her Sunday easel. Whatever the marks turn out to be, the brush has not been put away.

qa.q: On which day did Chitra plan to keep painting during exams?
qa.a: Chitra planned to keep painting on Sundays.

qa.q: What was Chitra feeling while she explained her plan, according to Vikas?
qa.a: Anxious but determined, since her voice was steady while her hands were tight around the sketchbook.

qa.q: What could Chitra do if exam stress makes Sundays impossible?
qa.a: Cut down to a short sketch or pause with a set return date, because it keeps a link with the hobby.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the change?
qa.a: As a sensible adaptation and not giving up, which is why Vikas reserved her wall space and easel.

grounding: A girl reduces painting to Sundays for exams, planning to return afterwards, adapting the routine instead of quitting.

subtype: Approach: trying several hobbies and never settling [Pitfall]
passage: At the community centre notice board, Irfan signed up for football on Mondays, guitar on Wednesdays and coding on Fridays, all in the first week of the month. By week three his calendar was full and his fingertips hurt, his football boots were always in the wrong bag, and the coding puzzle still showed the same error. Coach Harish watched him miss an easy pass. "Your mind is somewhere else, Irfan." "Everywhere else," Irfan muttered. On Friday he stared at the blank screen, felt his shoulders sag and thought maybe he was just no good at anything. He shut the laptop and left before the class ended.

qa.q: Which three activities did Irfan sign up for?
qa.a: Irfan signed up for football, guitar and coding.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel on Friday while staring at the blank screen?
qa.a: Discouraged, since his shoulders sagged and he thought he might be no good at anything.

qa.q: What could Irfan try instead of three activities at once?
qa.a: Pick one activity for a month and return to the others later, because focused time brings visible progress.

qa.q: How might Coach Harish see the missed pass?
qa.a: As a sign that Irfan is stretched too thin, since Harish said Irfan's mind was somewhere else.

grounding: A child begins football, guitar and coding in a single month and, with too little time for each, makes little progress and loses heart.

subtype: Approach: pairing the hobby with an existing habit [Thinking]
passage: Chinmayi dropped her school bag. "I keep forgetting to read," she told her father Mohit, who was folding laundry. "Every night I say I will start, and then I am asleep." "Hmm," said Mohit. "What is the one thing I never forget?" she asked herself aloud. "Brushing my teeth. Every night, even when I am sleepy." Mohit raised an eyebrow. "So if I read right after brushing... the brushing reminds me!" "Try it," said Mohit. That night she put her story book on the shelf by the mirror, brushed, then sat on the bed with it. A week later Mohit said, "You did not even remind yourself tonight." "Brush, then book," said Chinmayi, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Chinmayi put her story book?
qa.a: She put it on the shelf by the mirror.

qa.q: What was Chinmayi feeling at the start about her reading?
qa.a: Frustrated with herself, since she kept saying she would begin and then fell asleep.

qa.q: What else could Chinmayi use as a cue for the habit?
qa.a: She could read right after packing her bag for the next day, because attaching a new habit to a daily one makes it easier to remember.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the new habit?
qa.a: With quiet pride, since he noticed she no longer needed reminding. 🙂

grounding: A girl attaches reading to brushing her teeth at night, a task she already does daily, so it is easier to remember.

subtype: Approach: setting a mini goal to show family [Action]
passage: Monday. Asif's magic book was full of tricks, but he had finished none of them. "Diwali is in three weeks," he told his cousin Deepika on the phone. "I will do three tricks for everyone." Now he had a deadline. The next Saturday Asif practised the coin trick twenty times in front of the mirror, dropped the coin nine times, and started a tick chart. Diwali night. In the living room, in front of all the cousins, his hand shook a little, but the coin vanished on the first try. Deepika clapped her hands and screamed, "Do it again!" By the third trick his grin was wider than anyone's.

qa.q: How many tricks did Asif plan to perform?
qa.a: Asif planned to perform three tricks.

qa.q: How did Asif feel in front of his cousins, and what showed it?
qa.a: Nervous but excited, since his hand shook a little yet he was grinning by the third trick.

qa.q: What could Asif do if a trick fails on Diwali night?
qa.a: Laugh, make it part of the show and move on to the next trick, because his practice has prepared him.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the show?
qa.a: Delighted and impressed, since she screamed and asked for the coin trick again.

grounding: A boy learning magic sets a mini goal to perform three tricks for cousins on Diwali, and the deadline shapes his practice.

subtype: Approach: choosing a hobby by what he enjoys not what is popular [Thinking]
passage: Sunday night. My friend Yogesh asked which hobby I am picking and I said cricket, because everyone does. Then on the roof this evening I asked myself: what do I do when nobody is watching? I watch the koel in the neem tree. I count the sparrows at the water bowl. Once I spent an hour on a mynah with a torn feather. Cricket I like when others cheer. So maybe my hobby should be the one I would do alone. Bird watching. Yogesh said "Boring!" and laughed, but not meanly. I will borrow Papa's old binoculars and start a notebook. Maybe Yogesh will come one morning. Harish

qa.q: What does Harish plan to borrow from Papa?
qa.a: Harish plans to borrow Papa's old binoculars.

qa.q: What question did Harish ask on the roof, and what feeling did the answer bring?
qa.a: "What do I do when nobody is watching?" The answer brought clarity and a bit of excitement about bird watching. 🙂

qa.q: How could Harish stay close to friends who love cricket?
qa.a: Invite Yogesh on a morning bird walk and still join a cricket game now and then, because a hobby of one's own need not cost friendships.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about Harish's choice?
qa.a: Surprised, since Yogesh called it boring, but not unkind, since Yogesh laughed gently and may turn curious later.

grounding: Harish asks what feels enjoyable when nobody watches and picks bird watching over cricket, choosing a hobby of Harish's own.

subtype: Approach: adjusting when the schedule feels like a burden [Revision]
passage: "Papa, I am changing my chart," Kavitha announced, flute case in hand. Hemant looked up. "Why?" "Seven days makes it homework. Yesterday I played badly on purpose so it would finish sooner." "That does not sound like fun." "It is not! So four days: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday. The other days I play only what I feel like." "Will you keep to four?" "Yes, and I will tick them." She stuck the new chart over the old one. On Wednesday, with no rule at all, she picked up the flute anyway and played a film tune for ten happy minutes.

qa.q: Which four days did Kavitha choose?
qa.a: Kavitha chose Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling about seven-day practice, and what showed it?
qa.a: Resentful and bored, since she played badly on purpose so that it would finish sooner.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do if four days starts to feel like a chore too?
qa.a: Shorten the sessions or vary what she plays, because enjoyment is what keeps her going.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Kavitha's change?
qa.a: With patience and understanding, since he asked questions and let her decide, and he can see she still wants to play.

grounding: A girl finds daily practice makes the hobby a chore, so she cuts it to four days and leaves the others for free play.

subtype: Approach: working backward from exam dates and syllabus weight [Thinking]
passage: Voice note for Rafiq, from Pema. You asked how I even started on boards, so listen. First I counted backwards starting from the exam in March, week by week, and found I had about twenty-two weeks. Then I wrote every chapter of every subject beside its marks weightage from the syllabus sheet. That was the surprise: Science and Maths hold the biggest share, and I had been giving Social Science the same time as them. So I gave the early mornings, when my head is clear, to Science and Maths, and moved the lighter subjects to the evening. I taped the count of weeks over my desk. It does not make the syllabus smaller, but now it looks like a mountain with steps.

qa.q: How many weeks did Pema count before the March exam?
qa.a: Pema counted about twenty-two weeks.

qa.q: What did Pema feel on discovering the marks weightage?
qa.a: Surprised, and probably a little worried, because time had been spread evenly while the marks were not.

qa.q: What could Pema do if early mornings stop working?
qa.a: Review after a week and move the hard subjects to another clear-headed time, because the plan should follow energy.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Pema's plan?
qa.a: As clear and useful because it turns a big syllabus into steps, though Rafiq may wonder whether early mornings would suit everyone.

grounding: A Class 10 student counts backwards from the exam date, ranks chapters by marks weight and gives the most hours to Science and Maths.
